web_blocks.html: The long-run account is one of a severe early trough followed by a marked industrial recovery. The price-blind consolidated history shows revenue falling from ₹597 crore in FY2015 to ₹380 crore in FY2017, with losses in FY2016–FY2018. Revenue reached ₹797 crore in FY2022, ₹1,001 crore in FY2024, ₹1,279 crore in FY2025 and ₹1,856 crore in FY2026. PAT moved from a loss of ₹14 crore in FY2018 to ₹45 crore in FY2021, ₹118 crore in FY2024, ₹175 crore in FY2025 and ₹239 crore in FY2026. Growth and margin expansion are real; they began from a depressed base, so the 5-year growth rate should not be read as an eternal run rate [1][1].

The operating-margin bridge is more important than the headline revenue CAGR. Operating margins were around 2–3% in FY2015–FY2018, 7% in FY2019–FY2020, 12% in FY2021–FY2022, 15% in FY2023, 17% in FY2024 and 18% in FY2025–FY2026. That broad step-up fits higher scale, export mix, engineering leverage and utilization. It is also exposed to the inverse: input inflation, unfavorable product mix, commissioning delays and lower factory absorption. CRISIL notes the ability to pass through raw-material price increases as a strength, but actual timing and degree of pass-through are not quantified in public accounts [1][9].

The newest audited year confirms profitability but reveals cash-flow tension. Consolidated FY2026 sales were ₹1,856.2 crore and PAT ₹238.8 crore. Consolidated CFO was ₹129.1 crore, only about 54% of PAT, compared with CFO ₹39.5 crore and PAT ₹174.6 crore in FY2025. Investing outflow was ₹101.9 crore in FY2026, chiefly fixed assets, intangibles and leasehold land, leaving free cash flow roughly ₹27 crore before financing and other investing items. The Screener-derived cash-flow table gives FCF ₹19 crore on its definition; the two series differ by line-item treatment, so this chapter uses audited CFO and direct disclosed capex rather than pretending one FCF convention is universal [1][1].

Working capital explains the divergence. Consolidated FY2026 trade receivables increased by ₹287.9 crore, inventory by ₹126.5 crore and other receivables by ₹2.9 crore. Trade payables added ₹178.5 crore and other payables/provisions added ₹87.7 crore, but total working-capital changes still absorbed ₹151.1 crore before tax. Debtor days increased from 125 in FY2025 to 146 in FY2026 in the supplied fundamentals; cash conversion cycle was 189 days in FY2025 and 173 in FY2026. The improvement in CCC is welcome but does not erase the large absolute funding need [1][1].

Balance-sheet leverage is low in formal borrowings, but working capital is the economic funding requirement. The supplied balance-sheet snapshot shows borrowings of ₹12 crore at March 2025 and ₹18 crore at March 2026, dropping to zero at September 2026 after capital raises. CRISIL reported ₹199 crore cash/liquid investments at March 2026, nil term debt and a ₹1,062 crore tangible net worth for the group. The audited balance sheet also contains substantial current liabilities, trade payables, customer advances and lease liabilities, so “almost debt free” should not be mistaken for a business with no funding needs [9][9].

Capital expenditure accelerated as the company entered its next capacity phase. Consolidated cash payments in FY2026 were approximately ₹104.2 crore for property, plant, equipment and CWIP, ₹4.3 crore for intangibles and ₹2.1 crore for leasehold land. Gross fixed assets and capital work in progress expanded; the annual report attributes rising depreciation and amortization to new assets and capacity expansion. Maintenance and growth capex are not separated in enough detail to calculate an exact maintenance-capex floor [1][1].

Return ratios improved sharply: the fundamentals snapshot shows ROCE rising from 2% in FY2015 to 16% in FY2022, 25% in FY2024, 30% in FY2025 and 34% in FY2026; FY2026 ROE is 24.7%. These are attractive reported numbers, but they measure a business at a point of high margins and strong demand. The company does not publish an independently derived weighted-average cost of capital or product-line ROIC, so an exact spread over WACC cannot be asserted here. A disciplined reader should test whether ROCE stays high after expanded capital, working capital and QIP proceeds are fully deployed [1][1].

Share count has also changed. The company split ₹2 shares into ₹1 shares in August 2026; after the split, a promoter preferential issue of 12.5 lakh shares at ₹600 per share raised ₹75 crore, and an October 2026 QIP of 77.42 lakh shares at ₹775 raised about ₹600 crore. These shares increase the denominator and strengthen liquidity, while also diluting prior holders. The split is not economic dilution; the two equity issuances are. Any later per-share analysis must use the post-issue capital base [2].

Earnings quality therefore earns a conditional reading. Audited profitability is strong and the company has modest borrowings, but working-capital absorption, capital expenditure and subsidiary impairment reduce the fraction of accounting profit that arrives as discretionary cash. A sustainable path would show CFO/PAT improving over a multi-year cycle, CCC and debtor days stabilizing or falling, and incremental capex yielding more shipments without margins slipping. If the order boom continues while receivables and inventory keep outrunning sales, the business could still remain profitable but become less self-funding [9][1][1].

web_blocks.caption: TD Power Systems: balance-sheet and funding history, FY2015–September 2026
web_blocks.takeaway: Borrowings are low, but other liabilities and working-capital assets have expanded with growth. The September 2026 column is interim; it should not be compared with audited year-end values as if dates were identical.

web_blocks.caption: TD Power Systems: cash-flow conversion and free cash flow, FY2015–FY2026
web_blocks.takeaway: CFO and FCF are volatile and often far below accounting earnings. Expansion capex and operating working capital make cash conversion a central test of the growth thesis.

web_blocks.caption: TD Power Systems: working-capital and return ratios, FY2015–FY2026
web_blocks.takeaway: Debtor days, inventory days, cash-conversion cycle and ROCE are taken directly from the same-session financial snapshot. The working-capital cycle remains long even as reported returns improve.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Profit has improved dramatically, but FY2026 converts only a little over half of consolidated PAT into operating cash before expansion spending. The next proof point is not another record quarter; it is a multi-year reduction in the gap between earnings and collections while new capacity earns its cost of capital.
